> 不出戶，知天下；不窺牖，見天道。其出彌遠，其知彌少.

Chapter 46 was about wanting: want more, and the calamity is greater.

Chapter 47 is about looking: look more, and you know less.

Two lines that sound like magic — know the world without leaving the room, see the way without looking out the window.

But the whole thing rests on two characters, and they are completely concrete.

## 窺 is to look through a small opening

窺: 小視也 — to look through a slit, to see through a small aperture.

牖: 穿壁以木為交窗也 — a hole cut in the wall, with wooden bars crossed to make a window.

A window in that period was a lattice. You looked through it, and you always saw two things: the scene outside, and the grid in front.

So 不窺於牖 does not mean "don't look." It means: don't look through that aperture.

Through a frame, you see the part that fits the frame. Always that part.

## 其出彌遠，其知彌少

The further one goes out, the less one knows.

This is not a paradox about travel. It is the arithmetic of framing: every additional aperture is another grid, and each grid delivers a portion while presenting it as the view.

Go further and you collect more portions, and the portions are all shaped by their frames. The accumulation of framed views is not knowledge of the whole; it is a larger collection of crops.

## 不行而知，不見而名，不為而成

> 是以聖人不行而知，不見而名，不為而成.

Without traveling, he knows; without looking, he names; without acting, he completes.

名 here is not "to give a name" in the labeling sense. It is to make a thing evident — 名 as in 有名, to bring something into clear definition.

The three lines describe one operation from three angles: the knowing is not assembled from parts, the naming is not applied from outside, the completion is not manufactured.

## Why this is not mystical

The claim has a boring, testable version.

Most of what a person believes about "the world" is assembled from framed views: reports, feeds, conversations with people who share the frame. The assembly produces confidence, and the confidence scales with the number of crops.

The alternative is not omniscience. It is: stop treating the crops as the view, and let the thing that is not a crop be legible.

That is 不出戶 — not staying home as a discipline, but not mistaking the aperture for the world.

## The relation to chapter 48

Chapter 48 will say: learning adds daily, the way subtracts daily.

Chapter 47 is the visual version of the same movement. Adding apertures is 為學; removing the frame from the seeing is 為道.

The two chapters are adjacent because they are the same insight described with the eye and with the hand.

## A test

Take one strong opinion you hold about a large subject. Ask which aperture it came through, and what that aperture structurally cannot show. The answer is usually specific and rarely flattering.
